title: The French Revolution

cards.h: A prison with seven prisoners became the symbol of a revolution
cards.b:
On 14 July 1789, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, a fortress prison. They wanted gunpowder. Inside, there were only seven prisoners.

But the Bastille stood for royal power, and its fall shook Europe.

France was broke after wars (including helping America). Society had three Estates: clergy, nobles, and everyone else. The Third Estate paid most taxes and had the least say. Bad harvests made bread dear.

In May 1789 Louis XVI called the Estates-General to raise money. The Third Estate declared itself a National Assembly and took the Tennis Court Oath (20 June).

The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August 1789) said men are born free and equal. In October, thousands of Parisian women marched to Versailles and brought the royal family to Paris.

In 1793 France was at war with most of Europe and torn by civil war. The Committee of Public Safety, with Robespierre, ruled by fear. The guillotine was used on thousands. Around 17,000 were officially executed; many more died in prisons and revolts, with some estimates of 40,000 deaths.

In July 1794 Robespierre himself was guillotined.

The revolutionaries abolished feudal privileges, made a new calendar and metric measures, and confiscated Church lands. 'Liberty, equality, fraternity' became the motto.

Women did not win the vote. Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman in 1791 and was guillotined in 1793.

The chaos ended with a young general taking power in 1799: Napoleon. Historians still argue whether the Revolution brought freedom or just a new strongman.

But after 1789, kings everywhere had to worry about what their people might do.

Myth: Marie Antoinette said it when told that the poor had no bread.Fact: no evidence she said it. A similar line appears in Rousseau's Confessions, written when she was a child, about 'a great princess'. It is propaganda.

Also, the Bastille's taking was not about freeing prisoners, and the Revolution did not end the monarchy overnight; it happened over three years.

Five things to remember

  1. The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789.
  2. The Declaration of Rights came in August 1789.
  3. Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
  4. The Terror lasted 1793-94.
  5. Napoleon took power in 1799.

Think about it

  • Why do revolutions often turn violent?
  • Who was left out of 'liberty, equality, fraternity'?
